hints: Notice the four names given: meson, positron, proton and quark. Ask yourself which of these are built from quarks and which are fundamental.
Recall that leptons are fundamental particles and include the electron and its antiparticle, while hadrons such as mesons and baryons are composite particles made of quarks.
Compare each name to those two groups: check quark content of the meson and proton, and check whether a quark itself can be a lepton.
walkthrough: Identify the groups to sort: leptons are fundamental particles that are not made of quarks, with examples being electrons, muons, neutrinos and their antiparticles.
Recall the hadron group: hadrons are composite particles made of quarks, including mesons made of one quark and one antiquark, and baryons such as the proton made of three quarks.

Apply this to the options: meson contains quarks so it is a hadron, proton contains three quarks so it is a hadron, and quark is the building block of hadrons and forms its own separate fundamental family.
The remaining particle, the positron, is the antielectron with charge $+e$. It is fundamental, is not made of quarks, and belongs with the electron in the lepton family.
Therefore the particle that satisfies the definition of a lepton is the positron. This is option B.

options.A: A meson is a hadron made of a quark and an antiquark, not a fundamental lepton.
options.B: A positron is the antiparticle of the electron and belongs to the lepton family of fundamental particles.
options.C: A proton is a baryon hadron made of three quarks ($uud$), not a lepton.
options.D: A quark is a fundamental particle but belongs to the quark family, distinct from the lepton family.
